headline: Efficient and resilient systems for machine learning across the computing continuum
intro: The cost of executing a model, measured in energy, in hardware, and in latency, increasingly determines where that model can be deployed and which institutions can afford to use it. PEARL investigates the runtime systems, memory hierarchies, schedulers, and compilers that govern this cost. Our objective is to make demanding inference and training workloads tractable on the hardware that is actually available, from embedded and wearable devices through edge infrastructure to warehouse-scale computers.
closing: Efficiency in this setting is a question of access rather than of engineering elegance. The performance and energy characteristics of a system determine whether a given capability remains confined to well-provisioned data centres or becomes available in a clinic, a classroom, a field station, or a handheld device.

thrusts.title: Efficient serving of large generative models
thrusts.stake: Inference, rather than training, now dominates the aggregate energy and capacity cost of deployed models.
thrusts.blurb: Training a large model is a bounded expense incurred once; serving it is an unbounded expense incurred across billions of invocations. Our work restructures the serving stack along four axes: asynchronous overlap of CPU and GPU execution to eliminate idle time on either processor, reorganisation and reuse of the key-value cache, elimination of token-level redundancy that does not affect the output, and selection of numerical precision per layer and per timestep rather than uniformly across the model.
highlights: APEX — asynchronous CPU–GPU execution for online LLM inference on memory-constrained GPUs
dLLM-Serve — memory management for diffusion language model serving
HiRED — attention-guided token dropping for high-resolution vision–language models
DiffPro — joint timestep and layer-wise precision optimisation for diffusion inference
HydraCache — long-context prefill parallelisation via distributed cache blending

thrusts.title: Inference at the edge and across the continuum
thrusts.stake: Latency budgets, intermittent connectivity, and data-governance constraints frequently preclude offloading inference to a data centre.
thrusts.blurb: Applications in clinical monitoring, industrial inspection, and radio access networks require inference within millisecond budgets, often over unreliable links, and frequently on data that cannot lawfully or safely leave the device on which it was acquired. We study how to partition a model across device, edge server, and cloud tiers, and how to determine what should be quantised, what should be speculatively executed, and what should be transmitted. The resulting systems place the latency-critical computation adjacent to the point of measurement and invoke remote resources only when the accuracy benefit justifies the cost.
highlights: SWEET — workload-balanced edge inference via quantisation and partitioning (NSF, with QUB and UCD)
SLED and WISP — speculative decoding and SLO-aware batching for distributed edge serving
Polymorph — energy-constrained multi-label classification of video streams on embedded devices
MARVEL — automated generation of model-class aware custom RISC-V extensions
Accelerating transformer inference on RISC-V for edge deployment
O-RAN slicing — scaling and placement of edge servers for next-generation wireless

thrusts.title: Memory systems and accelerator utilisation
thrusts.stake: Accelerator capacity is scarce and costly, yet utilisation in production deployments remains substantially below the achievable maximum.
thrusts.blurb: An accelerator dedicated to a single tenant is typically underutilised, and a working set that exceeds fast memory reduces the throughput of an entire job to that of the slowest tier in the hierarchy. Neither condition is remedied by additional hardware, since both arise from scheduling and memory-management policy rather than from insufficient capacity. We develop mechanisms for safe spatial sharing of accelerators among concurrent workloads, for predicting page access ahead of demand faults, and for placing data across memory tiers without requiring explicit programmer intervention.
highlights: ParvaGPU — spatial GPU sharing for large-scale DNN inference in cloud environments
Stride-aware page prefetching for GPU unified memory via Markov pattern prediction
Memory tiering within the Python virtual machine
Application-attuned memory management for containerised HPC workflows

thrusts.title: Agentic methods for high-performance code optimisation
thrusts.stake: Scientific software commonly attains a fraction of the performance its target hardware permits, and the expertise required to close that gap is scarce.
thrusts.blurb: Computational science codes are written predominantly by domain scientists rather than performance engineers, and the resulting gap between attained and achievable performance is frequently an order of magnitude. We develop multi-agent systems that analyse such code, propose transformations, evaluate them empirically, and retain only those changes that are validated by measurement. Establishing confidence in machine-generated optimisations requires benchmarks and correctness guarantees, which we treat as a component of the research rather than as an afterthought. Undergraduate researchers contribute substantially to this effort.
highlights: MARCO — multi-agent code optimisation for high-performance computing
FACT — compositional CUDA kernel synthesis grounded in CUTLASS C++
LLM-guided runtime parameter optimisation for energy-efficient inference
AI-driven autonomous experimentation for turbulent flows
Parallel Islands — an educational instrument for parallel computing

thrusts.title: Resilience and energy accounting at scale
thrusts.stake: At scale, hardware faults are routine rather than exceptional, and energy consumption constitutes a first-order design constraint.
thrusts.blurb: A system that returns an incorrect result without indication, or that consumes its power budget without accounting for it, presents a more serious problem than one that fails observably. We characterise energy consumption at the granularity of execution stage, input modality, and instruction, and we develop recovery mechanisms that permit a long-running computation to survive component failure without restarting from its initial state. The intent is to render the cost and the correctness of a computation predictable before substantial machine time is committed to it.
highlights: Modality inflation — energy characterisation of multimodal LLM inference
Power Log'n'Roll — power-efficient localised rollback for MPI applications
SAFIRE — compiler-driven parallel fault injection (with LLNL)
Dynamic precision iterative refinement
